Drawing on empirical data and case studies, this section synthesizes information from different sources to examine the impact of linguicism on linguistic minority defendants in the criminal justice system.

Berk-Seligson (2009) conducted an experimental investigation into the effects of limited English proficiency (LEP) on native Spanish speakers who took part in mock trials with English-speaking police officers, attorneys, and jurors. Results revealed that police officers were more likely to perceive LEP defendants as less intelligent, persuasive, and truthful than their English-speaking counterparts. Furthermore, jurors attributed lower credibility to LEP defendants, demonstrating how language barriers can lead to prejudiced assessments of defendants’ character and reliability.

Shuy (1993) studied cases involving African American defendants who faced communication barriers due to the use of African American Vernacular English (AAVE). Misinterpretation of AAVE by White attorneys led to misunderstandings and inadequate legal representation, negatively impacting defendants’ outcomes. This suggests that linguistic differences, even within the same language, can contribute to unequal treatment within the criminal justice system.

Giles and Niedzielski (1998) found that people with nonstandard accents were more likely to be negatively evaluated by jurors, even when they were proficient in the legal system’s dominant language. Jurors’ perceptions were influenced by stereotypes associated with specific accents, leading to biased assessments of credibility and competence. This highlights how linguistic prejudice extends beyond language proficiency and may be deeply rooted in cultural and societal factors.

Nakane (2014) studied the interpreter-mediated interactions in police interviews in Japan and found that deficiencies in interpreting services contributed to discrepancies in understanding legal procedures, miscommunication, and limitations in defendants’ participation in their defense. This raises concerns about the effectiveness of current interpreting services in ensuring fair treatment for linguistic minority defendants.

Eades (2010) analyzed the experiences of Indigenous defendants in Australia’s criminal justice system, identifying significant challenges arising from language barriers and cultural differences. The study showed that communication difficulties arising from language differences and interpreter issues were exacerbated by cultural misunderstandings, racism, and stereotypes about Indigenous Australians.

Fabela v. State of Illinois (1975) is a landmark case in which an interpreter failed to provide accurate translations, leading to the conviction of a non-English-speaking defendant on charges that carried a life sentence. This case illustrates the potential for miscarriages of justice due to inadequate translation and interpreting services.

Types of Intellectual Property as per WIPO are:

Copyright

Patents

Trademarks

Industrial Designs

Geographical Indications

Trade secrets

Copyright

Copyright is a legal term used to describe the rights that creators have over their literary and artistic works.
Works covered by copyright range from books, music, paintings, sculpture and films, to computer
programs, databases, advertisements, maps and technical drawings.

Patents
A patent is an exclusive right granted for an invention. Generally speaking, a patent provides the patent
owner with the right to decide how - or whether - the invention can be used by others. In exchange for this
right, the patent owner makes technical information about the invention publicly available in the published
patent document.

Trademarks
A trademark is a sign capable of distinguishing the goods or services of one enterprise from those of other
enterprises. Trademarks date back to ancient times when artisans used to put their signature or “mark” on
their products.
8

Types of IP continue

Industrial designs
An industrial design constitutes the ornamental or aesthetic aspect of an article. A design may consist of
three-dimensional features, such as the shape or surface of an article, or of two-dimensional features, such
as patterns, lines or colour.

Geographical Indications
Geographical indications and appellations of origin are signs used on goods that have a specific
geographical origin and possess qualities, a reputation or characteristics that are essentially attributable to
that place of origin. Most commonly, a geographical indication includes the name of the place of origin of
the goods.

Trade Secrets
Trade secrets are IP rights on confidential information which may be sold or licensed. The unauthorized
acquisition, use or disclosure of such secret information in a manner contrary to honest commercial
practices by others is regarded as an unfair practice and a violation of the trade secret protection.

A father and son in Massachusetts will spend years in prison for a decade-long lottery scam that saw them claim $20 million in winnings from 14,000 tickets, illegally obtained from the true winners. Authorities are calling it "an elaborate tax fraud" that ensnared not only the father and son but a second son and "a vast network of co-conspirators," including convenience store owners, per CNN. According to the US Attorney's Office in Boston, the defendants illegally purchased lottery tickets from winners who opted for a discounted price so as to avoid identification by the state lottery commission, which is required to "withhold any outstanding taxes, back taxes, and child support payments before paying out prizes."

Ali Jaafar, 63, and Yousef Jaafar, 29, of Watertown would claim the lottery prizes as their own, helped by convenience store owners whom they "recruited and paid ... to facilitate the transactions," prosecutors say. The pair cashed over 14,000 tickets "from at least 2011 through at least June 2020." It was hard not to notice. In 2019, Ali Jaafar was the highest individual ticket casher in the state. His son, Mohamed, was the third highest, and Yousef was the fourth highest. They further profited by "reporting the winnings on their income tax returns and claiming equivalent fake gambling losses as an offset." They reported federal tax losses of more than $6 million and ended up collecting $1.2 million in fraudulent tax refunds.

A federal jury convicted Ali and Yousef of one count of conspiracy to defraud the IRS, one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering, and one count of filing a false tax return in December, before sentencing was handed down Monday. Ali received five years in prison, while Yousef received four years and two months. They are also required to forfeit their profits and pay more than $6 million in restitution. Mohamed Jaafar pleaded guilty to conspiracy to defraud the IRS in November and is due to be sentenced in July, per CBS News. Prosecutors note that more than 40 lottery retailers who participated in the scheme will see their lottery agent licenses revoked.
